# UKIP 2001 General Election Manifesto Summary

## Core Position: EU Withdrawal

The UK Independence Party, founded in 1993, positions itself as the only political party genuinely committed to British sovereignty and withdrawal from the European Union. UKIP frames the EU as a "confidence trick" that has transformed from the promised "Common Market" of 1973 into a centralised, bureaucratic superstate threatening British independence, legal traditions, and democratic self-governance.

## The "Independence Dividend"

Central to UKIP's economic argument is the claimed £20 billion annual "Independence Dividend" from leaving the EU—comprising £8.5 billion in direct budget contributions plus £11.5 billion from deregulation benefits, reduced bureaucracy, and restored fishing revenues. This would fund increased pensions (£5/week), NHS investment (£2 billion), 30,000 additional teachers, 25,000 more police, enhanced defence spending, and 40p/gallon fuel duty reductions.

## Economic Vision

UKIP advocates free-market principles, genuine global free trade liberated from EU protectionism, and regulatory "bonfires" particularly benefiting small businesses. They oppose euro adoption permanently, viewing it as an instrument of political integration rather than economic benefit. Tax simplification and reduced burdens on lower earners feature prominently.

## Public Services

The manifesto calls for NHS decentralisation, restoration of traditional "matron" management structures, and freedom from EU-imposed regulations. Education policy emphasises traditional teaching methods, selection by ability, reduced class sizes, and elimination of "politically correct" curricula and EU "brainwashing."

## Sovereignty and Identity

UKIP presents itself as defending British common law, trial by jury, parliamentary supremacy, and constitutional monarchy against EU legal harmonisation (particularly "Corpus Juris"). They oppose regionalisation as EU-driven "balkanisation" while supporting firm immigration controls and expedited asylum processing—policies they argue EU membership prevents.

The manifesto frames independence not as isolationism but as enabling stronger Commonwealth and global relationships.
